{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a comprehensive summary table of published manipulation benchmarks that could be rerun on a low-cost robot arm. Include columns for: Benchmark Name, Category (ISO/NIST/Pick-and-Place/Lab Task/Low-Cost), Protocol Summary, Measured Metrics, Number of Trials, Robot Arm(s) Used, Key Quantitative Result, Gripper/Sensor, Replicable on Low-Cost Arm?, Publication Type (journal/conference/preprint), and DOI. Include the following benchmarks from the evidence gathered:

1. ISO 9283 Pose Accuracy & Repeatability - Pollák et al. 2020 - UR5, 30 cycles, AP=0.022mm, RP≤0.065mm, Heidenhain MT25 sensors
2. ISO 9283-inspired Force Benchmarking - Kirschner et al. 2021 - UR5e/UR10e/Franka Panda, 30 repetitions, force accuracy/repeatability, K6D40 F/T sensor
3. NIST Assembly Task Board #1 - Lian et al. 2021 - KUKA IIWA14/ABB IRB1200/UR5e, 12 parts, peg-in-hole
4. IndustReal NIST-inspired Assembly - Tang et al. 2023 - Franka Panda, 600 trials, 83-99% success, RealSense D435
5. DR.J Electronic Task Board (Robothon) - So et al. 2024 - Multiple platforms including Franka, 10 teams, 6 subtasks, timing
6. Comparative Peg-in-Hole - Van Wyk et al. 2018 - 60 insertions per system, 3D-printed pegs
7. YCB Benchmarking Protocols - Calli et al. 2015 - Any arm, 60 trials for peg-insertion, YCB object set
8. Box and Blocks Test - Morgan et al. 2020 - Barrett WAM/Franka Panda, ≥5 repetitions, 16-100 blocks
9. SceneReplica - Khargonkar et al. 2024 - 20 scenes, 16 YCB objects, pick-and-place
10. GRASPA 1.0 - Bottarel et al. 2020 - iCub/Franka Panda, 5 trials per object, YCB subset, lift+hold success
11. FurnitureBench - Heo et al. 2025 - Franka Panda, 10 trials, furniture assembly, parallel gripper
12. ArmnetBench v0.1 - Selvaraj et al. 2026 - SO-101, 2518 rollouts, 12 tasks, 7 policies (PREPRINT)
13. SO-101 ACT Scaling - Cowling 2026 - SO-101, 1340 episodes, pick-and-place with distractors (PREPRINT)
14. LabRobFail - Wang et al. 2026 - Chemical SDL, 20k+ trajectories, 70+ tasks, failure analysis (PREPRINT)
15. RobInHood SDL - Longley et al. 2026 - Franka Panda, vial/decap/solid/liquid handling, fume hood
16. MATTERIX - Darvish et al. 2025 - KUKA KMR iiwa, 90% success in real-world experiments
17. ADePT Framework - Salazar-Villacis & Benyahia 2026 - Framework scoring 4 dimensions: Adaptability, Dexterity, Perception, Task Complexity
18. Cable Loop Gripper - Manes et al. 2024 - KUKA iiwa, ≤1% grasp failure rate, cylindrical/prismatic objects"}

{"answer": "## Repeatable Benchmarks for Validating Low-Cost Robot Arms as Automated Manual Manipulators in Self-Driving Laboratories

### 1. Introduction

This review identifies published manipulation benchmarks with quantitative results on industrial or research robot arms that could be reproduced on low-cost platforms (AgileX PiPER, SO-101) equipped with parallel grippers and RGB cameras. The benchmarks span six categories: (1) ISO 9283 pose metrology, (2) NIST-inspired task-board and peg-in-hole assembly, (3) pick-and-place with standardized objects, (4) laboratory-specific sample handling, (5) low-cost arm policy benchmarks, and (6) capability-assessment frameworks. Where no published evidence exists for a particular comparison, that gap is stated explicitly. All benchmarks are compiled in the table below.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### 2. ISO 9283 Pose Accuracy and Repeatability

The fundamental metrological benchmark for any robot arm is EN ISO 9283:1998, which prescribes commanding the tool centre point (TCP) to five points inside an imaginary ISO cube across at least 30 unidirectional cycles. Pollák et al. (2020) performed this measurement on a Universal Robots UR5 using six Heidenhain MT 25 / MT 12 incremental sensors (stated accuracy 0.004 mm) and six VRZ 401 evaluation units (pqac-00000071, pqac-00000072). Under 100 % payload at 10 % speed, the measured unidirectional pose accuracy was AP = 0.02223 mm; observed repeatability values ranged from approximately 0.033 mm to 0.065 mm across conditions, well within the ±0.1 mm manufacturer specification (pqac-00000069, pqac-00000070). Kirschner et al. (2021) adapted the ISO 9283 methodology for force-sensing benchmarking on a Franka Emika Panda, UR5e, and UR10e, using a K6D40 force–torque sensor (500 N range, 0.2 % accuracy) and 30 repetitions per condition (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001). Their results measure force accuracy and repeatability, not Cartesian pose, so they must not be conflated with pose-repeatability specifications (pqac-00000002).

**Replication guidance for low-cost arms:** A simplified version using an AprilTag fiducial target and an external camera to measure TCP position over 30+ cycles can yield useful pose-repeatability data, but should not be claimed as fully ISO-equivalent without adequate traceability and uncertainty analysis. PiPER, with its higher build quality, is a more suitable candidate than SO-101 for this test.

### 3. NIST-Inspired Task Boards and Peg-in-Hole Assembly

**Lian et al. (2021, IROS)** benchmarked off-the-shelf solutions on NIST Assembly Task Board #1, selecting 12 parts (four round pegs of 4–16 mm, four rectangular pegs, and four connectors including USB and RJ45) and evaluating position control (KUKA iiwa 14), hybrid force/motion control with spiral search (ABB IRB1200 with ATI Gamma F/T sensor), and 3-D vision (UR5e with LMI Gocator 3506 sensors) (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006). The protocol injects controlled 3-D pose perturbations and measures completion rate, tolerance area, cycle time, and cost. Per-task success rates were not available in the retrieved text but are reported in the paper's figures.

**Tang et al. (2023, preprint)** presented IndustReal using a Franka Emika Panda with a wrist-mounted Intel RealSense D435 camera and reinforcement-learning policies trained in simulation. Over 600 real-world trials on NIST-inspired pegs and gears with 0.5–0.6 mm clearances, success rates ranged from 83 % to 99 %: specifically, pick achieved 158/160 (98.75 %), insertion 100/120 (83.33 %), and complete pick–place–insert 107/120 (89.16 %) (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000043).

**So et al. (2024, IEEE RAM)** introduced the Digital Robot Judge (DR.J), a compact electronic task board with six industry-inspired subtasks (button press, key switch, Ethernet-plug insertion, battery extraction, battery recycling, and button press). Across two international Robothon competitions, 10 of 29 selected teams completed all tasks. The board automatically records subtask completion times. The best robot achieved 52 s versus a human mean of 18.9 s and best of 8.1 s. Robots reached only 16 % of best-human speed overall, though one specialized task was completed 9× faster than humans (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030). Platforms included Franka, KUKA iiwa, and Epson VT6 (pqac-00000028). The DR.J board is modular and openly documented, making it particularly attractive for low-cost arm validation.

**Van Wyk et al. (2018, IEEE T-RO)** compared compliant-hand and rigid-end-effector peg-in-hole strategies using 3-D-printable pegs at dimensionless clearance c = 0.02, with 60 attempted insertions per system and Gaussian positional offsets of 1 and 2 mm standard deviation (pqac-00000003).

### 4. Pick-and-Place and YCB Object Protocols

**Calli et al. ### 2. ISO 9283 Pose Accuracy and Repeatability

The fundamental metrological benchmark for any robot arm is EN ISO 9283:1998, which prescribes commanding the tool centre point (TCP) to five points inside an imaginary ISO cube across at least 30 unidirectional cycles. Pollák et al. (2020) performed this measurement on a Universal Robots UR5 using six Heidenhain MT 25 / MT 12 incremental sensors (stated accuracy 0.004 mm) and six VRZ 401 evaluation units (pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 10-12, pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 1-2). Under 100 % payload at 10 % speed, the measured unidirectional pose accuracy was AP = 0.02223 mm; observed repeatability values ranged from approximately 0.033 mm to 0.065 mm across conditions, well within the ±0.1 mm manufacturer specification (pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 12-14, pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 16-18). Kirschner et al. (2021) adapted the ISO 9283 methodology for force-sensing benchmarking on a Franka Emika Panda, UR5e, and UR10e, using a K6D40 force–torque sensor (500 N range, 0.2 % accuracy) and 30 repetitions per condition (kirschner2021towardsareference pages 3-4, kirschner2021towardsareference pages 2-3). Their results measure force accuracy and repeatability, not Cartesian pose, so they must not be conflated with pose-repeatability specifications (kirschner2021towardsareference pages 1-2).

**Replication guidance for low-cost arms:** A simplified version using an AprilTag fiducial target and an external camera to measure TCP position over 30+ cycles can yield useful pose-repeatability data, but should not be claimed as fully ISO-equivalent without adequate traceability and uncertainty analysis. PiPER, with its higher build quality, is a more suitable candidate than SO-101 for this test.

### 3. NIST-Inspired Task Boards and Peg-in-Hole Assembly

**Lian et al. (2021, IROS)** benchmarked off-the-shelf solutions on NIST Assembly Task Board #1, selecting 12 parts (four round pegs of 4–16 mm, four rectangular pegs, and four connectors including USB and RJ45) and evaluating position control (KUKA iiwa 14), hybrid force/motion control with spiral search (ABB IRB1200 with ATI Gamma F/T sensor), and 3-D vision (UR5e with LMI Gocator 3506 sensors) (lian2021benchmarkingofftheshelfsolutions pages 1-2, lian2021benchmarkingofftheshelfsolutions pages 3-4, lian2021benchmarkingofftheshelfsolutions pages 2-3). The protocol injects controlled 3-D pose perturbations and measures completion rate, tolerance area, cycle time, and cost. Per-task success rates were not available in the retrieved text but are reported in the paper's figures.

**Tang et al. (2023, preprint)** presented IndustReal using a Franka Emika Panda with a wrist-mounted Intel RealSense D435 camera and reinforcement-learning policies trained in simulation. Over 600 real-world trials on NIST-inspired pegs and gears with 0.5–0.6 mm clearances, success rates ranged from 83 % to 99 %: specifically, pick achieved 158/160 (98.75 %), insertion 100/120 (83.33 %), and complete pick–place–insert 107/120 (89.16 %) (tang2023industrealtransferringcontactrich pages 1-2, tang2023industrealtransferringcontactrich pages 8-10, tang2023industrealtransferringcontactrich pages 2-3).

**So et al. (2024, IEEE RAM)** introduced the Digital Robot Judge (DR.J), a compact electronic task board with six industry-inspired subtasks (button press, key switch, Ethernet-plug insertion, battery extraction, battery recycling, and button press). Across two international Robothon competitions, 10 of 29 selected teams completed all tasks. The board automatically records subtask completion times. The best robot achieved 52 s versus a human mean of 18.9 s and best of 8.1 s. Robots reached only 16 % of best-human speed overall, though one specialized task was completed 9× faster than humans (so2024digitalrobotjudge pages 8-9, so2024digitalrobotjudge pages 11-13, so2024digitalrobotjudge pages 9-10). Platforms included Franka, KUKA iiwa, and Epson VT6 (so2024digitalrobotjudge pages 11-13). The DR.J board is modular and openly documented, making it particularly attractive for low-cost arm validation.

**Van Wyk et al. (2018, IEEE T-RO)** compared compliant-hand and rigid-end-effector peg-in-hole strategies using 3-D-printable pegs at dimensionless clearance c = 0.02, with 60 attempted insertions per system and Gaussian positional offsets of 1 and 2 mm standard deviation (wyk2018comparativepeginholetesting pages 3-5).

### 4. Pick-and-Place and YCB Object Protocols

**Calli et al. (2015, IEEE RAM)** defined the YCB Object and Model Set benchmarking framework, including a Peg Insertion Learning Assessment (60 trials: 40 at the known home position across four time limits of 0.5–5 s, plus 20 trials at unknown 5/10 mm perturbations), a Gripper Assessment, Block Pick and Place, Table Setting, and a Pitcher-Mug pouring task. On the HERB robot, the Pitcher-Mug protocol was completed successfully in 8/10 configurations (calli2015benchmarkinginmanipulationa pages 24-27, calli2015benchmarkinginmanipulation pages 11-13, calli2015benchmarkinginmanipulationa pages 11-13). These protocols are hardware-agnostic and directly replicable.

**Morgan et al. (2020, IEEE RA-L)** adapted the clinical Box and Blocks Test (BBT) for robot benchmarking, defining three protocols: Modified-BBT (16 ordered blocks), Targeted-BBT (16 blocks placed in numbered targets), and Standard-BBT (transfer from 100 randomly configured blocks in one minute). Each protocol is repeated at least five consecutive times. Baselines were provided on a Barrett WAM with a Yale OpenHand T42 gripper and a Franka Emika Panda with extended parallel-gripper fingers (morgan2020benchmarkingclutteredrobot pages 1-2, morgan2020benchmarkingclutteredrobot pages 4-5). The BBT apparatus is distributed with the YCB Object and Model Set, ensuring reproducibility.

**Bottarel et al. (2020, IEEE RA-L)** presented GRASPA 1.0, evaluating five physical grasps per object per layout with a success criterion of lifting 0.15 m and holding for at least 5 s. Example iCub results included mustard bottle and chips can at 100 %, banana and cracker box at 80 %, and foam brick and tennis ball at 20 % (bottarel2020graspa1.0graspa pages 3-4, bottarel2020graspa1.0graspa pages 7-8). The benchmark was also deployed on a Franka Emika Panda with a RealSense D415 camera (bottarel2021wheresmymesh? pages 64-67, bottarel2021wheresmymesh? pages 84-87).

**Heo et al. (2025, IJRR)** presented FurnitureBench, a reproducible long-horizon benchmark using a 7-DOF Franka Emika Panda with its default parallel gripper, three RealSense D435 cameras, and AprilTags. Skills were evaluated over 10 trials; example IQL success rates reached 100 % for some desk grasp/place phases. Reproduced environments in 10 newly built setups retained 84 % of original performance (heo2025furniturebenchreproduciblerealworld pages 6-7, heo2025furniturebenchreproduciblerealworld pages 8-10, heo2025furniturebenchreproduciblerealworld pages 3-4). Single-skill components (grasping, insertion) are transferable to low-cost arms, though full furniture assembly may exceed their payload.

**Khargonkar et al. (2024, ICRA)** introduced SceneReplica, using 20 procedurally generated cluttered tabletop scenes with 16 YCB objects, designed for reproducibility without AR tags (khargonkar2024scenereplicabenchmarkingrealworld pages 1-2).

### 5. Laboratory-Specific Manipulation Tasks

**RobInHood (Longley et al. 2026, Digital Discovery)** demonstrated a Franka Emika Panda performing vial transport, capping/decapping (via a fixture-based friction rail), solid dispensing, liquid dispensing, heating/stirring, filtration, and imaging of 20 mL sample vials within a standard fume hood (longley2026robinhoodarobotic pages 3-5). No repeated-trial success rate was reported in the extracted evidence; this is an explicit gap that makes direct quantitative comparison with low-cost arms impossible without establishing such rates.

**Manes et al. (2024, Scientific Reports)** reported a soft cable-loop gripper on a KUKA iiwa for chemistry automation that achieved a failure rate of only 0.8 %, summarized as ≤1 % grasp failures, for cylindrical and prismatic laboratory objects. The exact trial denominator was not available from the extracted evidence.

**MATTERIX (Darvish et al. 2025, Nature Computational Science)** achieved a 90 % success rate in real-world experiments using a KUKA KMR iiwa mobile manipulator for chemistry-laboratory tasks, evaluated through a digital-twin simulation-to-real pipeline. Full protocol details would need to be recovered from the paper before replication.

**LabRobFail (Wang et al. 2026, preprint)** provides a benchmark for robotic failure analysis in chemical self-driving laboratories, with more than 20,000 operation trajectories covering 70+ task scenarios (pick, place, pour, stir, dryer loading), five major failure categories (Perception, Grasping, Motion, Logic, Safety), and 11 fine-grained failure types. Their VLM-based failure-detection system achieved 90.83 % accuracy and improved downstream task success by 4–16 percentage points (wang2026labrobfailabenchmark pages 2-3, wang2026labrobfailabenchmark pages 1-2).

**ADePT Framework (Salazar-Villacis & Benyahia 2026, Communications Chemistry)** proposes a four-dimensional assessment for autonomous laboratory robots: Adaptability and Learning, Dexterity, Perception, and Task Complexity. Example dexterity tasks include vial manipulation, sealing, pipetting, microwell-plate insertion, and pouring (salazarvillacis2026theadeptframework pages 4-5, salazarvillacis2026theadeptframework pages 6-7, salazarvillacis2026theadeptframework pages 2-3). ADePT is a scoring rubric, not a physical test suite, and must be paired with repeated-trial protocols.

**No published evidence exists** for standardized, repeated-trial benchmarks of vial decapping, microplate loading, or instrument-loading success rates with quantitative denominators on any arm model. The SDL literature describes these tasks qualitatively but does not report manipulation success rates in a form that permits cross-platform comparison. This is the most significant gap identified.

### 6. Low-Cost Arm Benchmarks

**ArmnetBench v0.1 (Selvaraj et al. 2026, preprint)** evaluated seven manipulation policies over 12 tasks (stacking, insertion, deformables, pick-and-place, articulated objects) on SO-101 arms, collecting 2,518 valid policy rollouts with approximately 30 rollouts per task–policy pair. Policy-only strict success was 690/2,518 ≈ 27.4 %, or 30.9 % including suboptimal outcomes (selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 3-7, selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 1-3). This is the most comprehensive published benchmark for the SO-101 platform.

**Cowling (2026, preprint)** tested four imitation-learning policies on a pick-and-place task (green ball into basket, two red distractors) using an SO-101 arm over 1,340 physical episodes. ACT achieved 2.5 % (1/40) with 12 demonstrations and rose to 92.5 % (37/40) with 100 demonstrations; fine-tuned π0.5 achieved 40 % at 12 and 70 % at 25 demonstrations (cowling2026from12to pages 1-3).

**LeRobot (Cadène et al. 2026, preprint)** provides the software ecosystem for SO-100/101 arms and reports approximate hardware costs: SO-100/101 at ~$225 ($550 for leader-follower pair), Koch-v1.1 at ~$670, ALOHA at ~$21k, and LeKiwi at ~$230 (cadene2026lerobotanopensource pages 3-5). The paper emphasizes that these platforms cost a fraction of the Franka Panda but does not state an exact Panda price.

### 7. Cost and Cost-Per-Task

**No published cost-per-task metric was found** in any of the reviewed literature. Tom et al. (2024, Chemical Reviews) provide approximate hardware-cost tiers for SDL platforms: special-purpose commercial hardware ~$1 M, general-purpose commercial hardware ~$10,000, and open hardware ~$100–$2,000 (tom2024selfdrivinglaboratoriesfor pages 5-6). Lo et al. (2024, Digital Discovery) describe the "frugal twin" concept and list representative system costs ranging from $300 (Educational ARES) to $15,000 (nanomaterials robot), with the Opentrons OT-2 at ~$7,500 (lo2024reviewoflowcost pages 5-6, lo2023reviewoflowcost pages 2-5). These are system-level figures, not isolated arm prices or per-task cost comparisons. This represents a significant gap: there is no published framework for normalizing a robot arm's hardware cost by the number of successful task completions to yield a cost-per-task metric. Developing such a metric (e.g., hardware amortization per successful vial transfer or peg insertion) would be a novel contribution.

### 8. Summary and Recommendations

The table above compiles 18 published benchmarks across six categories. For validating a PiPER or SO-101 as an automated manual manipulator in a self-driving laboratory, the following benchmark stack is recommended, ordered from foundational to application-specific:

1. **Pose repeatability** (simplified ISO 9283 with AprilTag fiducial, 30+ cycles)
2. **Peg-in-hole insertion** (3D-printed NIST-style pegs, 60+ trials per clearance, following Van Wyk et al. or IndustReal geometry)
3. **DR.J electronic task board** (automatic scoring of 6 subtasks including insertion and manipulation)
4. **YCB pick-and-place** (BBT protocol, ≥5 repetitions per condition, YCB block set)
5. **GRASPA grasping** (5 trials per YCB object, 0.15 m lift, 5 s hold)
6. **SDL-specific primitives** (vial pick-and-place, decapping, plate loading — these must be established as new benchmarks with ≥30 trials per primitive, since no published standard exists)
7. **LeRobot/ArmnetBench imitation-learning tasks** (for SO-101 specifically, using the published 12-task suite)

For each test, report the exact arm model, gripper, camera, control method (scripted vs. learned), number of trials, success criterion, and any fixture or environmental aids. Where a low-cost arm cannot match an industrial arm's native force sensing, state the limitation rather than omitting the benchmark.

### 2. ISO 9283 Pose Accuracy and Repeatability

The fundamental metrological benchmark for any robot arm is EN ISO 9283:1998, which prescribes commanding the tool centre point (TCP) to five points inside an imaginary ISO cube across at least 30 unidirectional cycles. Pollák et al. (2020) performed this measurement on a Universal Robots UR5 using six Heidenhain MT 25 / MT 12 incremental sensors (stated accuracy 0.004 mm) and six VRZ 401 evaluation units (pqac-00000071, pqac-00000072). Under 100 % payload at 10 % speed, the measured unidirectional pose accuracy was AP = 0.02223 mm; observed repeatability values ranged from approximately 0.033 mm to 0.065 mm across conditions, well within the ±0.1 mm manufacturer specification (pqac-00000069, pqac-00000070). Kirschner et al. (2021) adapted the ISO 9283 methodology for force-sensing benchmarking on a Franka Emika Panda, UR5e, and UR10e, using a K6D40 force–torque sensor (500 N range, 0.2 % accuracy) and 30 repetitions per condition (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001). Their results measure force accuracy and repeatability, not Cartesian pose, so they must not be conflated with pose-repeatability specifications (pqac-00000002).

**Replication guidance for low-cost arms:** A simplified version using an AprilTag fiducial target and an external camera to measure TCP position over 30+ cycles can yield useful pose-repeatability data, but should not be claimed as fully ISO-equivalent without adequate traceability and uncertainty analysis. PiPER, with its higher build quality, is a more suitable candidate than SO-101 for this test.

### 3. NIST-Inspired Task Boards and Peg-in-Hole Assembly

**Lian et al. (2021, IROS)** benchmarked off-the-shelf solutions on NIST Assembly Task Board #1, selecting 12 parts (four round pegs of 4–16 mm, four rectangular pegs, and four connectors including USB and RJ45) and evaluating position control (KUKA iiwa 14), hybrid force/motion control with spiral search (ABB IRB1200 with ATI Gamma F/T sensor), and 3-D vision (UR5e with LMI Gocator 3506 sensors) (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006). The protocol injects controlled 3-D pose perturbations and measures completion rate, tolerance area, cycle time, and cost. Per-task success rates were not available in the retrieved text but are reported in the paper's figures.

**Tang et al. (2023, preprint)** presented IndustReal using a Franka Emika Panda with a wrist-mounted Intel RealSense D435 camera and reinforcement-learning policies trained in simulation. Over 600 real-world trials on NIST-inspired pegs and gears with 0.5–0.6 mm clearances, success rates ranged from 83 % to 99 %: specifically, pick achieved 158/160 (98.75 %), insertion 100/120 (83.33 %), and complete pick–place–insert 107/120 (89.16 %) (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000043).

**So et al. (2024, IEEE RAM)** introduced the Digital Robot Judge (DR.J), a compact electronic task board with six industry-inspired subtasks (button press, key switch, Ethernet-plug insertion, battery extraction, battery recycling, and button press). Across two international Robothon competitions, 10 of 29 selected teams completed all tasks. The board automatically records subtask completion times. The best robot achieved 52 s versus a human mean of 18.9 s and best of 8.1 s. Robots reached only 16 % of best-human speed overall, though one specialized task was completed 9× faster than humans (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030). Platforms included Franka, KUKA iiwa, and Epson VT6 (pqac-00000028). The DR.J board is modular and openly documented, making it particularly attractive for low-cost arm validation.

**Van Wyk et al. (2018, IEEE T-RO)** compared compliant-hand and rigid-end-effector peg-in-hole strategies using 3-D-printable pegs at dimensionless clearance c = 0.02, with 60 attempted insertions per system and Gaussian positional offsets of 1 and 2 mm standard deviation (pqac-00000003).

### 4. Pick-and-Place and YCB Object Protocols

**Calli et al. (2015, IEEE RAM)** defined the YCB Object and Model Set benchmarking framework, including a Peg Insertion Learning Assessment (60 trials: 40 at the known home position across four time limits of 0.5–5 s, plus 20 trials at unknown 5/10 mm perturbations), a Gripper Assessment, Block Pick and Place, Table Setting, and a Pitcher-Mug pouring task. On the HERB robot, the Pitcher-Mug protocol was completed successfully in 8/10 configurations (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). These protocols are hardware-agnostic and directly replicable.

**Morgan et al. (2020, IEEE RA-L)** adapted the clinical Box and Blocks Test (BBT) for robot benchmarking, defining three protocols: Modified-BBT (16 ordered blocks), Targeted-BBT (16 blocks placed in numbered targets), and Standard-BBT (transfer from 100 randomly configured blocks in one minute). Each protocol is repeated at least five consecutive times. Baselines were provided on a Barrett WAM with a Yale OpenHand T42 gripper and a Franka Emika Panda with extended parallel-gripper fingers (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000016). The BBT apparatus is distributed with the YCB Object and Model Set, ensuring reproducibility.

**Bottarel et al. (2020, IEEE RA-L)** presented GRASPA 1.0, evaluating five physical grasps per object per layout with a success criterion of lifting 0.15 m and holding for at least 5 s. Example iCub results included mustard bottle and chips can at 100 %, banana and cracker box at 80 %, and foam brick and tennis ball at 20 % (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055). The benchmark was also deployed on a Franka Emika Panda with a RealSense D415 camera (pqac-00000059, pqac-00000060).

**Heo et al. (2025, IJRR)** presented FurnitureBench, a reproducible long-horizon benchmark using a 7-DOF Franka Emika Panda with its default parallel gripper, three RealSense D435 cameras, and AprilTags. Skills were evaluated over 10 trials; example IQL success rates reached 100 % for some desk grasp/place phases. Reproduced environments in 10 newly built setups retained 84 % of original performance (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037). Single-skill components (grasping, insertion) are transferable to low-cost arms, though full furniture assembly may exceed their payload.

**Khargonkar et al. (2024, ICRA)** introduced SceneReplica, using 20 procedurally generated cluttered tabletop scenes with 16 YCB objects, designed for reproducibility without AR tags (pqac-00000011).

### 5. Laboratory-Specific Manipulation Tasks

**RobInHood (Longley et al. 2026, Digital Discovery)** demonstrated a Franka Emika Panda performing vial transport, capping/decapping (via a fixture-based friction rail), solid dispensing, liquid dispensing, heating/stirring, filtration, and imaging of 20 mL sample vials within a standard fume hood (pqac-00000019). No repeated-trial success rate was reported in the extracted evidence; this is an explicit gap that makes direct quantitative comparison with low-cost arms impossible without establishing such rates.

**Manes et al. (2024, Scientific Reports)** reported a soft cable-loop gripper on a KUKA iiwa for chemistry automation that achieved a failure rate of only 0.8 %, summarized as ≤1 % grasp failures, for cylindrical and prismatic laboratory objects. The exact trial denominator was not available from the extracted evidence.

**MATTERIX (Darvish et al. 2025, Nature Computational Science)** achieved a 90 % success rate in real-world experiments using a KUKA KMR iiwa mobile manipulator for chemistry-laboratory tasks, evaluated through a digital-twin simulation-to-real pipeline. Full protocol details would need to be recovered from the paper before replication.

**LabRobFail (Wang et al. 2026, preprint)** provides a benchmark for robotic failure analysis in chemical self-driving laboratories, with more than 20,000 operation trajectories covering 70+ task scenarios (pick, place, pour, stir, dryer loading), five major failure categories (Perception, Grasping, Motion, Logic, Safety), and 11 fine-grained failure types. Their VLM-based failure-detection system achieved 90.83 % accuracy and improved downstream task success by 4–16 percentage points (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045).

**ADePT Framework (Salazar-Villacis & Benyahia 2026, Communications Chemistry)** proposes a four-dimensional assessment for autonomous laboratory robots: Adaptability and Learning, Dexterity, Perception, and Task Complexity. Example dexterity tasks include vial manipulation, sealing, pipetting, microwell-plate insertion, and pouring (pqac-00000063, pqac-00000066, pqac-00000067). ADePT is a scoring rubric, not a physical test suite, and must be paired with repeated-trial protocols.

**No published evidence exists** for standardized, repeated-trial benchmarks of vial decapping, microplate loading, or instrument-loading success rates with quantitative denominators on any arm model. The SDL literature describes these tasks qualitatively but does not report manipulation success rates in a form that permits cross-platform comparison. This is the most significant gap identified.

### 6. Low-Cost Arm Benchmarks

**ArmnetBench v0.1 (Selvaraj et al. 2026, preprint)** evaluated seven manipulation policies over 12 tasks (stacking, insertion, deformables, pick-and-place, articulated objects) on SO-101 arms, collecting 2,518 valid policy rollouts with approximately 30 rollouts per task–policy pair. Policy-only strict success was 690/2,518 ≈ 27.4 %, or 30.9 % including suboptimal outcomes (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000025). This is the most comprehensive published benchmark for the SO-101 platform.

**Cowling (2026, preprint)** tested four imitation-learning policies on a pick-and-place task (green ball into basket, two red distractors) using an SO-101 arm over 1,340 physical episodes. ACT achieved 2.5 % (1/40) with 12 demonstrations and rose to 92.5 % (37/40) with 100 demonstrations; fine-tuned π0.5 achieved 40 % at 12 and 70 % at 25 demonstrations (pqac-00000021).

**LeRobot (Cadène et al. 2026, preprint)** provides the software ecosystem for SO-100/101 arms and reports approximate hardware costs: SO-100/101 at ~$225 ($550 for leader-follower pair), Koch-v1.1 at ~$670, ALOHA at ~$21k, and LeKiwi at ~$230 (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000051). The paper emphasizes that these platforms cost a fraction of the Franka Panda but does not state an exact Panda price.

### 7. Cost and Cost-Per-Task

**No published cost-per-task metric was found** in any of the reviewed literature. Tom et al. (2024, Chemical Reviews) provide approximate hardware-cost tiers for SDL platforms: special-purpose commercial hardware ~$1 M, general-purpose commercial hardware ~$10,000, and open hardware ~$100–$2,000 (pqac-00000050). Lo et al. (2024, Digital Discovery) describe the "frugal twin" concept and list representative system costs ranging from $300 (Educational ARES) to $15,000 (nanomaterials robot), with the Opentrons OT-2 at ~$7,500 (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000052). These are system-level figures, not isolated arm prices or per-task cost comparisons. This represents a significant gap: there is no published framework for normalizing a robot arm's hardware cost by the number of successful task completions to yield a cost-per-task metric. Developing such a metric (e.g., hardware amortization per successful vial transfer or peg insertion) would be a novel contribution.

### 8. Summary and Recommendations

The table above compiles 18 published benchmarks across six categories. For validating a PiPER or SO-101 as an automated manual manipulator in a self-driving laboratory, the following benchmark stack is recommended, ordered from foundational to application-specific:

1. **Pose repeatability** (simplified ISO 9283 with AprilTag fiducial, 30+ cycles)
2. **Peg-in-hole insertion** (3D-printed NIST-style pegs, 60+ trials per clearance, following Van Wyk et al. or IndustReal geometry)
3. **DR.J electronic task board** (automatic scoring of 6 subtasks including insertion and manipulation)
4. **YCB pick-and-place** (BBT protocol, ≥5 repetitions per condition, YCB block set)
5. **GRASPA grasping** (5 trials per YCB object, 0.15 m lift, 5 s hold)
6. **SDL-specific primitives** (vial pick-and-place, decapping, plate loading — these must be established as new benchmarks with ≥30 trials per primitive, since no published standard exists)
7. **LeRobot/ArmnetBench imitation-learning tasks** (for SO-101 specifically, using the published 12-task suite)

For each test, report the exact arm model, gripper, camera, control method (scripted vs. learned), number of trials, success criterion, and any fixture or environmental aids. Where a low-cost arm cannot match an industrial arm's native force sensing, state the limitation rather than omitting the benchmark.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not report ISO 9283 pose repeatability or pose accuracy results for a UR5e, Franka Panda, or another standard industrial robot arm. It describes a custom venipuncture needle manipulator and provides related positioning data. Frequency-tracking experiments evaluated the manipulator’s joints independently using sine-wave inputs at 45, 90, and 180 deg/s, with 10° amplitude for revolute joints and 5 mm for the injection system. The reported mean standard deviation across all tracking tests was 0.005 mm, indicating high repeatability. Positioning accuracy and workspace were assessed by commanding the needle tip to the centers of 4 mm circles arranged on a rigid 7×7 calibration grid with 7 mm center-to-center spacing. The commanded locations were derived from the robot coordinate frame and CAD model, and actual needle-tip positions were compared against them. Measurement used fixed stereo near-infrared cameras; needle-tip segmentation involved region growing and a Canny edge detector, with manual post-processing to minimize errors. contexts.context: The excerpt reports a NIST-relevant comparative peg-in-hole benchmark involving two robotic strategies: a compliant robotic hand using a force-based manipulation controller, and a conventional approach using a rigid end-effector with a compliant or force-controlled robot arm. The protocol used a 3-D-printable peg-and-hole task with dimensionless clearance c = 0.02; holes were spaced approximately 35 cm apart. The test began with two pegs in two holes and required cyclic transfer of a peg into the next available hole. Each system performed 60 attempted insertions, with identical X–Y positional errors applied to both systems on every trial. Positional offsets were sampled from zero-mean Gaussian distributions with standard deviations of 1 mm and 2 mm. Performance was quantified using completion time (the alignment-plus-insertion time, excluding constant acquisition and transport) and probability of success. Success probability was calculated using sample and success counts with a 95% confidence level. The excerpt does not identify the specific robot-arm models, nor does it provide the numerical peg-in-hole success rates or completion-time results; those would need to be obtained from later results sections of the paper. contexts.context: This excerpt describes the protocol of Lian et al. (IROS 2021), a published benchmark of off-the-shelf solutions for robotic peg-in-hole assembly on a task board. It evaluates four metrics: reliability, usability, cycle time, and cost; reliability is measured using end-to-end task completion rate and a module-level tolerance area. The study considers 12 tasks with differing shapes, dimensions, and clearances. For intrinsic task difficulty, the peg begins inserted in its corresponding hole to reduce grasp uncertainty, a nominally aligned hole pose is defined, and controlled 3D perturbations are injected in in-plane translation (x and y) and in-plane rotation (rz), with possible out-of-plane effects (rx and ry) depending on clearance. Three insertion baselines are compared: position control, hybrid motion/force control with spiral search, and 3D-vision-guided position control. The listed robot platforms are a Kuka IIWA14 for Position, an ABB IRB1200 for Force, and a UR5e for 3DVision; the Force setup includes an ATI Gamma force-torque sensor, and the vision setup uses static and wrist-mounted LMI 3506 Gocators. contexts.context: The excerpt describes several quantitative YCB manipulation benchmarks, but it provides complete trial counts and success rates only for the Pitcher-Mug benchmark. That benchmark was run on the HERB robot and tested 10 pitcher–mug configurations; 8 of 10 were successfully completed. In the two failures, the robot could grasp the pitcher but could not generate a suitable pouring path. The benchmark scores performance by penalizing liquid remaining in the pitcher or spilled on the table. The YCB Gripper Assessment benchmark evaluates grasping across objects of various shapes and sizes from the YCB shape and tool categories. It compares Yale GRAB Lab grippers Model T and Model T42, rather than distinct robot arm models. Model T successfully grasps only a limited range of object sizes and is unsuitable for small, flat objects; Model T42 handles large-object power grasps, small-object precision grasps, and flat objects, but has disadvantages with articulated objects. The Table Setting benchmark uses a mug, fork, knife, spoon, bowl, and plate placed at predefined initial locations and moved to specified final configurations; scoring is based on final-pose accuracy and it can run in simulation using YCB URDF models. contexts.context: The excerpt describes the Morgan et al. Box and Blocks Test (BBT) protocols implemented with the YCB object set, but it does not provide arm-specific success-rate results, numbers of experimental trials, or robot arm models. The Modified-BBT (M-BBT) transfers 16 identically oriented blocks across a barrier in minimal time and primarily evaluates manipulator design and grasping. The Targeted-BBT (T-BBT) also uses 16 blocks, but requires accurate placement in specified target locations, thereby evaluating end-effector and manipulator accuracy and control. The Standard-BBT (S-BBT) transfers as many randomly configured blocks as possible out of 100 across the barrier; it has timed one-minute and untimed variants and additionally challenges perception, segmentation, planning, and grasp synthesis in clutter. M-BBT and T-BBT use templates with 16 colored blocks in four colors, while S-BBT uses 100 blocks with random placement and color distributions. The physical setup includes YCB objects #68 and #69. Reported quantitative metrics include score, blocks picked (S-BBT), pick attempts (S-BBT), end-effector distance, planning time, execution time, and total time. Thus, this excerpt establishes benchmark task sizes and evaluation variables, but not comparative success rates by arm, trial counts, or specific arm models.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the Box and Blocks Test (BBT) as a quantitative pick-and-place benchmark, but it does not report empirical success-rate results or YCB object-set protocols. It specifies that each task protocol should be repeated consecutively at least five times, with failed executions receiving a score of zero; planning, execution, and total time should also be reported. contexts.context: The excerpt identifies five YCB-based manipulation protocols that can serve as quantitative robot-arm benchmarks: Pitcher-Mug, Gripper Assessment, Table Setting, Block Pick and Place, and Peg Insertion Learning Assessment. The clearest reported pick-and-place-like success result is the Pitcher-Mug benchmark, run on the HERB robot arm: the task succeeded for 8 of 10 pitcher–mug configurations, while two failures involved grasping successfully but being unable to plan a suitable pouring path. The Table Setting benchmark uses YCB mug, fork, knife, spoon, bowl, and plate objects, places them at predefined initial locations, and evaluates accuracy of their final poses; it can also be run in Gazebo using supplied URDF models. The Block Pick and Place protocol tests grasping small blocks and transferring them to specified locations, assessing both arm/gripper hardware and motion planning. Its score combines task completion and placement precision, although the excerpt does not provide a numerical success rate or trial count. The Gripper Assessment benchmark compares grippers using YCB shape and tool objects, but the excerpt reports capability differences rather than arm-level trial totals. Thus, the excerpt provides a concrete 8/10 result for HERB and defines object sets and scoring criteria for additional benchmarks, but does not give complete numbers of trials, object counts, or distinct arm models for every protocol.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports a quantitative benchmark on a low-cost SO-101 arm, not SO-100 or other robot models. The tested manipulation task was a pick-and-place task involving two distractor objects. Policies were trained using nested subsets of 12, 25, 50, 100, and 200 teleoperated demonstrations, then evaluated on ten fixed object placements with a 30-second episode limit. Across all policies and checkpoints, the study scored 1,340 physical-robot episodes in 126 blocks over 17 days. ACT, trained from scratch, achieved 1/40 successes (2.5%) with 12 demonstrations and 37/40 (92.5%) with 100 demonstrations. Fine-tuned π0.5 performed best at low data volumes, achieving 16/40 (40%) at 12 demonstrations and 28/40 (70%) at 25 demonstrations, subsequently remaining near 70%. SmolVLA and Diffusion Policy each peaked near 50%, although their results were strongly affected by initiation failures: SmolVLA did not start moving in 47% of episodes, while Diffusion Policy generally failed to start until idle lead-in segments were removed from demonstrations. The excerpt gives no quantitative benchmark for SO-100 or additional low-cost arms.

The deployment used three cells: two single-arm SO-101 cells and one bimanual cell, with 2,520 benchmark rollouts collected (840 per cell); two were removed because of manual reset errors, leaving 2,518 policy rollouts. Because the 600 human reference episodes were successful by construction, the policy-only results can be derived as 690 successes, 89 suboptimal outcomes, and 1,739 failures among 2,518 policy rollouts: approximately 27.4% strict success, or 30.9% when suboptimal goal achievement is included. contexts.context: The excerpt reports aggregate DR.J Robothon Grand Challenge benchmark results for 2021 and 2022, but it does not provide arm-specific numerical completion times for a Franka Panda or other individual platforms. In 2021, 20 teams applied, nine were selected and sent task boards, and four successfully completed all tasks, giving a selected-team success rate of 4/9 (44.4%). In 2022, 27 teams applied, 20 were selected, and six completed all tasks, giving 6/20 (30.0%). Across both years, 10 of 29 selected teams completed the full trial protocol (34.5%). Each team had 30 days to develop its solution. The submitted benchmark evidence included an uncut recording of the robot solving the board five consecutive times, while final winners were determined from timing data collected during supervised demonstrations. The trial protocol contained six subtasks (press button, key switch, Ethernet plug, extract battery, recycle battery, and press button), and teams could perform them in any order. Quantitative timing values and platform-specific results are said to appear in Figures 7–8 and Tables 4–5, but those data are not included in this excerpt. The text notes that ST1 generally took the most time despite being judged among the least complex tasks.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports a reproducibility evaluation of FurnitureBench using a 7-DoF Franka Emika Panda arm with a default parallel gripper and three Intel RealSense D435 RGB-D cameras. A fully trained IQL-R3M policy was evaluated on the one_leg assembly task in 10 newly built environments. Performance was measured by the average number of completed subtasks (or phases), rather than by an explicitly stated binary task-success rate: the reproduced environments achieved, on average, 84% of the performance obtained in the original environment. Separately, 10 participants independently constructed the environments from scratch following the setup instructions, with each setup taking approximately 3 hours. The provided excerpt does not give the absolute number of trials, individual trial success rates, or a numerical count of successful versus failed complete assemblies. Thus, the quantitative results visible here are the 84% relative performance figure, evaluation across 10 new environments, and setup by 10 participants; any detailed success-rate and trial-count results would need to be obtained from other pages or tables in the paper.

Performance is averaged over T trials for each object and layout. For isolated-object tests, the per-object composite score combines grasp quality (S3), grasp stability (S5), and a binary execution-success factor (S4), yielding a score in [0, 2]. contexts.context: The excerpt reports GRASPA’s execution-based grasping success measure as a per-object success rate. Each grasp trial is binary: S4Lk,t equals 1 when object k is grasped and 0 otherwise. The reported object-level success score is the mean over T = 5 grasp executions, so the possible rates are 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, or 1.0 (0–100%). A grasp counts as successful only when the object can be lifted by 0.15 m and held without falling for at least five seconds. Contact slip is allowed provided it does not ultimately make the object fall. The benchmark permits evaluating this rate either with the object grasped in isolation or in a cluttered scene, but the same evaluation modality must be maintained for every object and layout. The excerpt also distinguishes this empirical execution score from graspability: S2 encodes whether the object is compatible with the robot’s payload and gripper aperture, rather than measuring repeated grasp success. No additional aggregate success rates across robots, objects, or layouts are given in these pages.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the GRASPA benchmark deployment protocol for a Franka Emika Panda arm, but it does not report an overall quantitative grasping success rate or the total number of physical grasp trials. Data collection was organized around GRASPA indicators: reachability (S0), camera calibration (S1), graspability (S2), and grasp quality (S3). For S0, the robot was positioned before the GRASPA board and reached targets while recording 6D end-effector poses through direct kinematics. For S1, a second Intel RealSense camera and markers attached to the robot hand were used to estimate the TCP pose and evaluate hand-camera calibration. For S2, objects with a smaller dimension exceeding 0.08 m were classified as ungraspable because this exceeded the Franka Hand’s maximum aperture. S3 was computed in Simox using a model of the hand and fingertip collision volumes; the authors varied the number of fingertip subdivisions and evaluated the same test grasp, including 50 perturbations, to study convergence of grasp quality. Thus, the excerpt supplies protocol details and a 50-perturbation evaluation count, but not benchmark-level success percentages or total trial counts.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes GRASPA’s quantitative grasp-execution and stability protocol but does not provide specific experimental success-rate values or a numerical number of trials for a particular robot or dataset. GRASPA includes a binary grasp-execution success score evaluated on physical robots. For stability, each grasp is tested over T trials while following a fixed five-waypoint trajectory: the initial grasp pose, rotations of +45° and −45° around the approach axis, a return orientation, and a 30° rotation toward the table. Each rotation trajectory has a reference duration of two seconds. The stability score is averaged over T trials as the fraction of the five waypoints reached without dropping the object; thus, each trial contributes Nw,reached/5, with Nw,tot = 5. Contact slip is allowed provided it does not cause the object to fall. The execution test may be conducted with isolated objects or in clutter, using the same modality for each object and layout. The excerpt also notes that graspability and obstacle-avoidance metrics are computed separately, and that non-graspable objects receive no score. Therefore, the supplied pages specify rates as benchmark score formulas and protocols, rather than reporting aggregate success percentages or an explicit T value.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies ADePT’s four robot-proficiency dimensions as Adaptability and Learning, Dexterity, Perception, and Task Complexity. It does not enumerate the specific benchmark tasks used to evaluate these dimensions; it directs readers to Supplementary Material SM2 for the scoring rubrics and SM3.2 for per-study evaluations. Within the excerpt, Dexterity is described as the ability to manipulate diverse laboratory objects accurately and controllably, including vials, pipettes, flasks, and specialized labware, sometimes in confined spaces or under delicate constraints. Perception concerns a robot’s ability to interpret its surroundings and use environmental information to respond to variation. Task Complexity concerns the capacity to perform complex, multi-step laboratory procedures rather than only fixed, pre-programmed actions. The passage also emphasizes that adaptability and learning involve generalizing skills across experimental protocols, responding to novel inputs, and refining behavior from experience. Examples mentioned include powder weighing and scraping, but these are presented as case studies of learning and dexterity—not explicitly as the complete ADePT benchmark task set. The framework is intended to distinguish structured automation from autonomy by assessing whether robots can perceive, adapt, manipulate equipment, and execute variable, complex workflows.
contexts.question: What benchmark tasks does the ADePT framework define for autonomous laboratory robotics, and what are the dexterity, perception, and task complexity dimensions?

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies ADePT as a conceptual benchmark for evaluating the core proficiencies needed for autonomous laboratory robotics. ADePT comprises four dimensions: Adaptability and Learning, Dexterity, Perception, and Task Complexity. The available text does not enumerate the framework’s specific benchmark tasks, so those tasks cannot be recovered from this excerpt alone. It does, however, indicate how three dimensions are treated. Dexterity concerns preserving device-level capabilities and constraints, particularly through information models that allow integrated systems to respect instrument limitations. Perception involves multimodal sensing—including vision, force sensing, and proximity detection—and operator-in-the-loop validation when scenes are ambiguous. Task Complexity concerns scaling interconnected workflows across instruments and sites, coordinating mixed-initiative human–robot operations, and increasing complexity without reducing safety or throughput. The excerpt also associates Adaptability and Learning with online reallocation, replanning, and human-guided updates. Overall, the framework is presented as a structured way to align robotic capabilities with the requirements of self-driving laboratories, rather than merely measuring isolated automation of repetitive procedures.
contexts.question: What benchmark tasks does the ADePT framework define for autonomous laboratory robotics, and what are the dexterity, perception, and task complexity dimensions?

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies three major ADePT assessment dimensions relevant to benchmark design: dexterity, perception, and task complexity. Dexterity concerns precise physical interaction with laboratory objects and instruments, including manipulation under tight tolerances, secure handling, well-plate insertion, vial manipulation, sealing, pipetting, and reactor interfacing. Perception covers object detection and localisation, experimental-state monitoring, environmental awareness, and feedback-driven adaptation. Relevant sensing includes vision, depth, LIDAR, force, and tactile feedback; important challenges include transparent vessels, occlusion, visual clutter, ambiguous signals, and changing temperature or humidity. Task complexity concerns the ability to execute multi-step protocols with precise sequencing, conditional decisions, adaptation to intermediate outcomes, planning under physical and temporal constraints, and recovery from uncertainty or failure. The excerpt’s representative benchmark-like workflows include a 12-step powder X-ray diffraction procedure involving sample preparation, transport, and data acquisition; execution across 20 modular stations covering reaction, analysis, and cleaning; and task-and-motion-planning scenarios involving object transport and pouring while avoiding collisions and spillage. It also notes that current systems often remain task-specific, rigid, and dependent on human intervention.
contexts.question: What benchmark tasks does the ADePT framework define for autonomous laboratory robotics, and what are the dexterity, perception, and task complexity dimensions?

contexts.context: The excerpt reports pose-accuracy and repeatability results for the UR5 tool-center-point measurement system, but it does not identify them as ISO 9283 measurements and does not state a number of measurement cycles. The measuring setup used the proposed Rhombicuboctahedron ArUco Mapper (RAM), consisting of multiple ArUco.3 fiducial markers observed by a camera. Absolute positional accuracy varied by test pose: the lowest reported accuracy was 0.4778 mm at P2, while the best values were approximately 0.1172 mm at P4 and 0.1762 mm at P5. Orientation accuracy ranged from 0.003° at P4 to 0.01° at P2. Repeatability was analyzed in the camera coordinate system using the same camera and computer, with the UR5 and camera kept in the same locations. The highest reported positional repeatability values were approximately 0.00006 mm at P4 and 0.00005 mm at P5; P2 had the lowest repeatability at 0.0005184 mm. Instead, it reports evaluation results for an H20 mobile robot system used for laboratory sample transport. The study conducted 60 runs comprising 300 activities: 120 grasping actions, 120 placing actions, and 60 activities on the robot frame. Fourteen activities failed, giving an overall repeatability of 95.33% and an overall failure rate of approximately 4.67%. Grasping had 9 failures out of 120, corresponding to 92.5% repeatability and a 7.5% failure rate. Placing had 5 failures out of 120, corresponding to 95.83% repeatability and an approximately 4.17% failure rate. The robot was equipped with dual arms, each described as having six joints plus a two-degree-of-freedom gripper. These figures may be useful as a comparison, but they should not be attributed to the Cooper/KUKA KMR iiwa system without another source.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not specifically identify the Cooper group’s mobile robotic chemist, the KUKA KMR iiwa platform, or report success rates by module. It does provide related quantitative results for the cable-loop gripper (CLG): a reliability test involved 1,000 vial manipulations using nine vials of three diameters, with tray movements and periodic cable-loop calibration. The prototype had a reported failure rate of 0.8%, and every failure occurred during grasping; no vial was lost during transport. The system operated for approximately 4.5 hours, with each manipulation taking about 8 seconds, and individual pick operations taking less than 5 seconds including visual servoing. In a separate environment-variability sorting test, the gripper successfully grasped all vials across five repetitions. The gripper type was a soft cable-loop-based gripper, designed to passively compensate for small placement errors while handling chemistry vials of different sizes.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the KUKA Mobile Robot (KMR), comprising a 7-DOF LBR iiwa arm and an omnidirectional KUKA Mobile Platform. For vial and rack manipulation, the study used an HGPLE electronic parallel gripper from Festo. The gripper was designed to handle 10 mL Agilent GC vials both from the top and sideways, including in tight spaces, and custom racks with 18 wells arranged in three rows of six. The study reports qualitatively that both vials and racks could be manipulated in various ways, and that the same gripper could grasp both. However, this excerpt does not report the Cooper group’s laboratory-wide quantitative success rates, the total number of experiments, or failure rates per module. It also does not identify those results as being specific to a Cooper group mobile robotic chemist evaluation.
contexts.question: What quantitative success rates were reported for the Cooper group mobile robotic chemist using KUKA KMR iiwa in the laboratory? How many experiments, what failure rate per module, and what gripper?

contexts.context: The excerpt reports that the earlier mobile-robot self-driving laboratory, attributed here to Benjamin Burger and reported in 2019, carried out more than 600 experiments. It used Bayesian optimisation and improved the hydrogen generation of a photocatalyst at a rate described as up to 1,000 times faster than a human researcher could achieve independently. The passage emphasizes that mobile-robot systems offer modularity and can be expanded with additional modules, but their complexity creates reliability problems. It does not provide quantitative failure rates for individual modules, nor does it identify the gripper used by the KUKA KMR iiwa. Although the excerpt later describes the KUKA KMR iiwa as the robotic researcher used in the project, the requested module-specific success/failure statistics and gripper details are not included in the supplied pages. The only directly reported experiment count is “over 600,” and the only quantitative performance comparison is the “1,000 times faster” photocatalyst-improvement claim.
contexts.question: What quantitative success rates were reported for the Cooper group mobile robotic chemist using KUKA KMR iiwa in the laboratory? How many experiments, what failure rate per module, and what gripper?

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: We are writing a literature review to discover which tests determine the value of a robot arm used as an automated manual manipulator in a self-driving laboratory (SDL) for materials science. By automated manual manipulator we mean one arm that does the hands-on work a person would otherwise do: it moves from station to station (for example a pipetting gantry, a powder doser, a balance, vial and plate racks), recalibrates itself at each station using a calibration square (a square fiducial target such as an AprilTag, or a square fixture at a known position), and takes on several new automated tasks. The term is ours; the literature may say mobile manipulator, robotic laboratory assistant, robot chemist, or sample- or labware-handling robot. Our arms are a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. We want to place these arms in the published literature and find tests that we, or anyone validating an affordable arm, can repeat to compare it with the industry-standard arms used in SDLs (e.g. UR5e, UR3, Franka Panda, ABB YuMi, Kinova, KUKA), including on cost per task.

Repeatable benchmarks: Which published manipulation benchmarks with quantitative results for industrial or research arms could be rerun on a low-cost arm with a parallel gripper and RGB cameras to judge it as an automated manual manipulator? Examples: ISO 9283 pose repeatability and accuracy, repeated pick-and-place success over N trials, peg-in-hole, NIST task boards, YCB object protocols, and laboratory tasks such as vial, plate and rack handling, decapping, and loading instruments.

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. For each benchmark or result, describe the protocol in enough detail to repeat it (what is measured, number of trials, success criterion, measuring tool) and give the arm model. For each claim, give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.


## Repeatable Benchmarks for Validating Low-Cost Robot Arms as Automated Manual Manipulators in Self-Driving Laboratories

### 1. Introduction

This review identifies published manipulation benchmarks with quantitative results on industrial or research robot arms that could be reproduced on low-cost platforms (AgileX PiPER, SO-101) equipped with parallel grippers and RGB cameras. The benchmarks span six categories: (1) ISO 9283 pose metrology, (2) NIST-inspired task-board and peg-in-hole assembly, (3) pick-and-place with standardized objects, (4) laboratory-specific sample handling, (5) low-cost arm policy benchmarks, and (6) capability-assessment frameworks. ### 2. ISO 9283 Pose Accuracy and Repeatability

The fundamental metrological benchmark for any robot arm is EN ISO 9283:1998, which prescribes commanding the tool centre point (TCP) to five points inside an imaginary ISO cube across at least 30 unidirectional cycles. Pollák et al. (2020) performed this measurement on a Universal Robots UR5 using six Heidenhain MT 25 / MT 12 incremental sensors (stated accuracy 0.004 mm) and six VRZ 401 evaluation units (pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 10-12, pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 1-2). Under 100 % payload at 10 % speed, the measured unidirectional pose accuracy was AP = 0.02223 mm; observed repeatability values ranged from approximately 0.033 mm to 0.065 mm across conditions, well within the ±0.1 mm manufacturer specification (pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 12-14, pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 16-18). Kirschner et al. (2021) adapted the ISO 9283 methodology for force-sensing benchmarking on a Franka Emika Panda, UR5e, and UR10e, using a K6D40 force–torque sensor (500 N range, 0.2 % accuracy) and 30 repetitions per condition (kirschner2021towardsareference pages 3-4, kirschner2021towardsareference pages 2-3). Their results measure force accuracy and repeatability, not Cartesian pose, so they must not be conflated with pose-repeatability specifications (kirschner2021towardsareference pages 1-2).

**Replication guidance for low-cost arms:** A simplified version using an AprilTag fiducial target and an external camera to measure TCP position over 30+ cycles can yield useful pose-repeatability data, but should not be claimed as fully ISO-equivalent without adequate traceability and uncertainty analysis. PiPER, with its higher build quality, is a more suitable candidate than SO-101 for this test.

### 3. NIST-Inspired Task Boards and Peg-in-Hole Assembly

**Lian et al. (2021, IROS)** benchmarked off-the-shelf solutions on NIST Assembly Task Board #1, selecting 12 parts (four round pegs of 4–16 mm, four rectangular pegs, and four connectors including USB and RJ45) and evaluating position control (KUKA iiwa 14), hybrid force/motion control with spiral search (ABB IRB1200 with ATI Gamma F/T sensor), and 3-D vision (UR5e with LMI Gocator 3506 sensors) (lian2021benchmarkingofftheshelfsolutions pages 1-2, lian2021benchmarkingofftheshelfsolutions pages 3-4, lian2021benchmarkingofftheshelfsolutions pages 2-3). The protocol injects controlled 3-D pose perturbations and measures completion rate, tolerance area, cycle time, and cost. Per-task success rates were not available in the retrieved text but are reported in the paper's figures.

**Tang et al. (2023, preprint)** presented IndustReal using a Franka Emika Panda with a wrist-mounted Intel RealSense D435 camera and reinforcement-learning policies trained in simulation. Over 600 real-world trials on NIST-inspired pegs and gears with 0.5–0.6 mm clearances, success rates ranged from 83 % to 99 %: specifically, pick achieved 158/160 (98.75 %), insertion 100/120 (83.33 %), and complete pick–place–insert 107/120 (89.16 %) (tang2023industrealtransferringcontactrich pages 1-2, tang2023industrealtransferringcontactrich pages 8-10, tang2023industrealtransferringcontactrich pages 2-3).

**So et al. (2024, IEEE RAM)** introduced the Digital Robot Judge (DR.J), a compact electronic task board with six industry-inspired subtasks (button press, key switch, Ethernet-plug insertion, battery extraction, battery recycling, and button press). Across two international Robothon competitions, 10 of 29 selected teams completed all tasks. The board automatically records subtask completion times. The best robot achieved 52 s versus a human mean of 18.9 s and best of 8.1 s. Robots reached only 16 % of best-human speed overall, though one specialized task was completed 9× faster than humans (so2024digitalrobotjudge pages 8-9, so2024digitalrobotjudge pages 11-13, so2024digitalrobotjudge pages 9-10). Platforms included Franka, KUKA iiwa, and Epson VT6 (so2024digitalrobotjudge pages 11-13). The DR.J board is modular and openly documented, making it particularly attractive for low-cost arm validation.

**Van Wyk et al. (2018, IEEE T-RO)** compared compliant-hand and rigid-end-effector peg-in-hole strategies using 3-D-printable pegs at dimensionless clearance c = 0.02, with 60 attempted insertions per system and Gaussian positional offsets of 1 and 2 mm standard deviation (wyk2018comparativepeginholetesting pages 3-5).

### 4. Pick-and-Place and YCB Object Protocols

**Calli et al. (2015, IEEE RAM)** defined the YCB Object and Model Set benchmarking framework, including a Peg Insertion Learning Assessment (60 trials: 40 at the known home position across four time limits of 0.5–5 s, plus 20 trials at unknown 5/10 mm perturbations), a Gripper Assessment, Block Pick and Place, Table Setting, and a Pitcher-Mug pouring task. On the HERB robot, the Pitcher-Mug protocol was completed successfully in 8/10 configurations (calli2015benchmarkinginmanipulationa pages 24-27, calli2015benchmarkinginmanipulation pages 11-13, calli2015benchmarkinginmanipulationa pages 11-13). These protocols are hardware-agnostic and directly replicable.

**Morgan et al. (2020, IEEE RA-L)** adapted the clinical Box and Blocks Test (BBT) for robot benchmarking, defining three protocols: Modified-BBT (16 ordered blocks), Targeted-BBT (16 blocks placed in numbered targets), and Standard-BBT (transfer from 100 randomly configured blocks in one minute). Each protocol is repeated at least five consecutive times. Baselines were provided on a Barrett WAM with a Yale OpenHand T42 gripper and a Franka Emika Panda with extended parallel-gripper fingers (morgan2020benchmarkingclutteredrobot pages 1-2, morgan2020benchmarkingclutteredrobot pages 4-5). The BBT apparatus is distributed with the YCB Object and Model Set, ensuring reproducibility.

**Bottarel et al. (2020, IEEE RA-L)** presented GRASPA 1.0, evaluating five physical grasps per object per layout with a success criterion of lifting 0.15 m and holding for at least 5 s. Example iCub results included mustard bottle and chips can at 100 %, banana and cracker box at 80 %, and foam brick and tennis ball at 20 % (bottarel2020graspa1.0graspa pages 3-4, bottarel2020graspa1.0graspa pages 7-8). The benchmark was also deployed on a Franka Emika Panda with a RealSense D415 camera (bottarel2021wheresmymesh? pages 64-67, bottarel2021wheresmymesh? pages 84-87).

**Heo et al. (2025, IJRR)** presented FurnitureBench, a reproducible long-horizon benchmark using a 7-DOF Franka Emika Panda with its default parallel gripper, three RealSense D435 cameras, and AprilTags. Skills were evaluated over 10 trials; example IQL success rates reached 100 % for some desk grasp/place phases. Reproduced environments in 10 newly built setups retained 84 % of original performance (heo2025furniturebenchreproduciblerealworld pages 6-7, heo2025furniturebenchreproduciblerealworld pages 8-10, heo2025furniturebenchreproduciblerealworld pages 3-4). Single-skill components (grasping, insertion) are transferable to low-cost arms, though full furniture assembly may exceed their payload.

**Khargonkar et al. (2024, ICRA)** introduced SceneReplica, using 20 procedurally generated cluttered tabletop scenes with 16 YCB objects, designed for reproducibility without AR tags (khargonkar2024scenereplicabenchmarkingrealworld pages 1-2).

### 5. Laboratory-Specific Manipulation Tasks

**RobInHood (Longley et al. 2026, Digital Discovery)** demonstrated a Franka Emika Panda performing vial transport, capping/decapping (via a fixture-based friction rail), solid dispensing, liquid dispensing, heating/stirring, filtration, and imaging of 20 mL sample vials within a standard fume hood (longley2026robinhoodarobotic pages 3-5). No repeated-trial success rate was reported in the extracted evidence; this is an explicit gap that makes direct quantitative comparison with low-cost arms impossible without establishing such rates.

**Manes et al. (2024, Scientific Reports)** reported a soft cable-loop gripper on a KUKA iiwa for chemistry automation that achieved a failure rate of only 0.8 %, summarized as ≤1 % grasp failures, for cylindrical and prismatic laboratory objects. The exact trial denominator was not available from the extracted evidence.

**MATTERIX (Darvish et al. 2025, Nature Computational Science)** achieved a 90 % success rate in real-world experiments using a KUKA KMR iiwa mobile manipulator for chemistry-laboratory tasks, evaluated through a digital-twin simulation-to-real pipeline. Full protocol details would need to be recovered from the paper before replication.

**LabRobFail (Wang et al. 2026, preprint)** provides a benchmark for robotic failure analysis in chemical self-driving laboratories, with more than 20,000 operation trajectories covering 70+ task scenarios (pick, place, pour, stir, dryer loading), five major failure categories (Perception, Grasping, Motion, Logic, Safety), and 11 fine-grained failure types. Their VLM-based failure-detection system achieved 90.83 % accuracy and improved downstream task success by 4–16 percentage points (wang2026labrobfailabenchmark pages 2-3, wang2026labrobfailabenchmark pages 1-2).

**ADePT Framework (Salazar-Villacis & Benyahia 2026, Communications Chemistry)** proposes a four-dimensional assessment for autonomous laboratory robots: Adaptability and Learning, Dexterity, Perception, and Task Complexity. Example dexterity tasks include vial manipulation, sealing, pipetting, microwell-plate insertion, and pouring (salazarvillacis2026theadeptframework pages 4-5, salazarvillacis2026theadeptframework pages 6-7, salazarvillacis2026theadeptframework pages 2-3). ADePT is a scoring rubric, not a physical test suite, and must be paired with repeated-trial protocols.

**No published evidence exists** for standardized, repeated-trial benchmarks of vial decapping, microplate loading, or instrument-loading success rates with quantitative denominators on any arm model. The SDL literature describes these tasks qualitatively but does not report manipulation success rates in a form that permits cross-platform comparison. This is the most significant gap identified.

### 6. Low-Cost Arm Benchmarks

**ArmnetBench v0.1 (Selvaraj et al. 2026, preprint)** evaluated seven manipulation policies over 12 tasks (stacking, insertion, deformables, pick-and-place, articulated objects) on SO-101 arms, collecting 2,518 valid policy rollouts with approximately 30 rollouts per task–policy pair. Policy-only strict success was 690/2,518 ≈ 27.4 %, or 30.9 % including suboptimal outcomes (selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 3-7, selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 1-3). This is the most comprehensive published benchmark for the SO-101 platform.

**Cowling (2026, preprint)** tested four imitation-learning policies on a pick-and-place task (green ball into basket, two red distractors) using an SO-101 arm over 1,340 physical episodes. ACT achieved 2.5 % (1/40) with 12 demonstrations and rose to 92.5 % (37/40) with 100 demonstrations; fine-tuned π0.5 achieved 40 % at 12 and 70 % at 25 demonstrations (cowling2026from12to pages 1-3).

**LeRobot (Cadène et al. 2026, preprint)** provides the software ecosystem for SO-100/101 arms and reports approximate hardware costs: SO-100/101 at ~$225 ($550 for leader-follower pair), Koch-v1.1 at ~$670, ALOHA at ~$21k, and LeKiwi at ~$230 (cadene2026lerobotanopensource pages 3-5). The paper emphasizes that these platforms cost a fraction of the Franka Panda but does not state an exact Panda price.

### 7. Cost and Cost-Per-Task

**No published cost-per-task metric was found** in any of the reviewed literature. Tom et al. (2024, Chemical Reviews) provide approximate hardware-cost tiers for SDL platforms: special-purpose commercial hardware ~$1 M, general-purpose commercial hardware ~$10,000, and open hardware ~$100–$2,000 (tom2024selfdrivinglaboratoriesfor pages 5-6). Lo et al. (2024, Digital Discovery) describe the "frugal twin" concept and list representative system costs ranging from $300 (Educational ARES) to $15,000 (nanomaterials robot), with the Opentrons OT-2 at ~$7,500 (lo2024reviewoflowcost pages 5-6, lo2023reviewoflowcost pages 2-5). These are system-level figures, not isolated arm prices or per-task cost comparisons. This represents a significant gap: there is no published framework for normalizing a robot arm's hardware cost by the number of successful task completions to yield a cost-per-task metric. Developing such a metric (e.g., hardware amortization per successful vial transfer or peg insertion) would be a novel contribution.

### 8. Summary and Recommendations

The table above compiles 18 published benchmarks across six categories. For validating a PiPER or SO-101 as an automated manual manipulator in a self-driving laboratory, the following benchmark stack is recommended, ordered from foundational to application-specific:

1. **Pose repeatability** (simplified ISO 9283 with AprilTag fiducial, 30+ cycles)
2. **Peg-in-hole insertion** (3D-printed NIST-style pegs, 60+ trials per clearance, following Van Wyk et al. or IndustReal geometry)
3. **DR.J electronic task board** (automatic scoring of 6 subtasks including insertion and manipulation)
4. **YCB pick-and-place** (BBT protocol, ≥5 repetitions per condition, YCB block set)
5. **GRASPA grasping** (5 trials per YCB object, 0.15 m lift, 5 s hold)
6. **SDL-specific primitives** (vial pick-and-place, decapping, plate loading — these must be established as new benchmarks with ≥30 trials per primitive, since no published standard exists)
7. **LeRobot/ArmnetBench imitation-learning tasks** (for SO-101 specifically, using the published 12-task suite)

For each test, report the exact arm model, gripper, camera, control method (scripted vs. learned), number of trials, success criterion, and any fixture or environmental aids. Where a low-cost arm cannot match an industrial arm's native force sensing, state the limitation rather than omitting the benchmark.

info.query:
We are writing a literature review to discover which tests determine the value of a robot arm used as an automated manual manipulator in a self-driving laboratory (SDL) for materials science. By automated manual manipulator we mean one arm that does the hands-on work a person would otherwise do: it moves from station to station (for example a pipetting gantry, a powder doser, a balance, vial and plate racks), recalibrates itself at each station using a calibration square (a square fiducial target such as an AprilTag, or a square fixture at a known position), and takes on several new automated tasks. The term is ours; the literature may say mobile manipulator, robotic laboratory assistant, robot chemist, or sample- or labware-handling robot. Our arms are a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. We want to place these arms in the published literature and find tests that we, or anyone validating an affordable arm, can repeat to compare it with the industry-standard arms used in SDLs (e.g. UR5e, UR3, Franka Panda, ABB YuMi, Kinova, KUKA), including on cost per task.

Repeatable benchmarks: Which published manipulation benchmarks with quantitative results for industrial or research arms could be rerun on a low-cost arm with a parallel gripper and RGB cameras to judge it as an automated manual manipulator? Examples: ISO 9283 pose repeatability and accuracy, repeated pick-and-place success over N trials, peg-in-hole, NIST task boards, YCB object protocols, and laboratory tasks such as vial, plate and rack handling, decapping, and loading instruments.

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. For each benchmark or result, describe the protocol in enough detail to repeat it (what is measured, number of trials, success criterion, measuring tool) and give the arm model. For each claim, give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.
